decks.title: Nature and Significance of Management — Part 1: Meaning, Objectives and Nature
goals: Explain management as a process and distinguish effectiveness from efficiency
Identify organisational, social and personal objectives in business situations
Explain the characteristics and importance of management
Evaluate management as a science, an art and a profession

slides.heading: Nature and Significance of Management
slides.body_md: Part 1: what management is, its **objectives**, **characteristics**, **importance**, and whether it is a **science, art or profession**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what management is, effectiveness and efficiency, objectives, characteristics, importance, and whether management is a science, an art or a profession
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Think of a school sports day. Somebody fixed the date, divided the work, chose volunteers, guided them and checked that every event started on time. That somebody was managing. In this chapter we ask what management really is, what it aims at, why every organisation needs it, and whether it is a science, an art or a profession.

slides.heading: What is management?
slides.body_md: **Management** is the process of getting things done **with and through others** to achieve goals **effectively and efficiently**.
bullets: **Process:** a series of functions (planning, organising, staffing, directing, controlling).
**Effectively:** the task is completed, on time.
**Efficiently:** resources are used at the lowest cost.

nodes.label: Goals achieved on time and at low cost

visual.alt: Flow: people and resources pass through the management process to goals achieved on time and at low cost

slides.narration: Managers rarely do the work themselves. They get it done through others. The definition has three key words. Process means a chain of functions. Effectively means the job is finished, and finished on time. Efficiently means it is finished without waste, at the lowest possible cost. Good management needs both, not just one.

visual.caption: Effectiveness is about the end result; efficiency is about cost.

slides.narration: Look at this grid. Effectiveness is about the result: did you meet the target on time? Efficiency is about the cost: did you avoid waste? A firm can meet its target but waste money, or save money but miss the target. Neither is good enough. Managers aim for the top right box, where the target is met on time and at low cost.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: effective, efficient or both?
slides.body_md: Four imagined units each had a target of 500 mats and a budget of ₹1 lakh.
bullets: Step 1: Compare output with the target. Met means **effective**.
Step 2: Compare cost with the budget. Within budget means **efficient**.
Step 3: Combine the two verdicts.

visual.alt: Table of four imagined units with target and output, budget and cost, and the verdict: Pune effective and efficient; Surat effective but not efficient; Patna efficient but not effective; Agra neither
visual.caption: Imagined figures. Compare output with target, then cost with budget.

slides.narration: Let us judge four imagined units. Pune made all 500 mats and spent less than budget, so it is effective and efficient. Surat met the target but overspent, so it is effective but not efficient. Patna saved money but made only 420 mats, so it is efficient but not effective. Agra missed the target and overspent, so it is neither. Always check the two things separately.

slides.heading: Quick check: two key words
slides.body_md: Fill in the two blanks about completing a task on time and at minimum cost.
slides.narration: Try this quick one. Which word goes with finishing on time, and which with keeping costs low?

slides.heading: Objectives of management

rows: Survival (cover costs), profit (reward risk), growth (sales, branches, products)
Quality goods at fair prices, eco-friendly methods, jobs for disadvantaged groups, community health or schools
Fair pay and benefits; recognition and good relations; training and growth

visual.alt: Table of the three objectives of management: organisational (survival, profit, growth), social (fair products, environment, jobs, community welfare) and personal (pay, recognition, growth of employees)

slides.narration: Management works towards three groups of objectives. Organisational objectives belong to the firm: survival, profit and growth. Social objectives belong to society: fair products, a clean environment, jobs and community welfare. Personal objectives belong to employees: fair pay, recognition and growth. A well managed firm balances all three.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: spotting the objective
slides.body_md: In a case, ask **whose need** is being met.
bullets: The firm itself: **organisational**.
The community or environment: **social**.
The employees: **personal**.

headers: Line from an imagined case (Tapti Textiles)
rows: Sales rose by a fifth and two new showrooms opened
Weavers were given a health plan and a supervisors' course
Dye waste is treated before it reaches the river
Prices were set to cover all costs with a fair margin

visual.alt: Worked example table: four lines from an imagined case matched to objectives: sales and showrooms show growth; health plan and course show personal objectives; treating dye waste shows a social objective; covering costs with a margin shows survival and profit
visual.caption: Underline the words that point to whose need is met.

slides.narration: Here are four lines from an imagined case about Tapti Textiles. Rising sales and new showrooms show growth, an organisational objective. A health plan and a supervisors course meet the needs of workers, so they are personal. Treating dye waste helps the river and the villages, so it is social. Covering costs with a fair margin means survival and profit.

slides.heading: Characteristics of management

visual.alt: Table of seven characteristics of management with key ideas: goal-oriented, pervasive, multidimensional, continuous, group activity, dynamic and intangible

slides.narration: Management has seven characteristics. It is goal oriented. It is pervasive, found in every kind of organisation. It is multidimensional, covering work, people and operations. It is continuous, because the functions repeat. It is a group activity. It is dynamic, adapting to change. And it is intangible: you cannot see it, but you can see its results.

slides.heading: Quick check: a characteristic
slides.body_md: Guests notice smooth service at a hotel but cannot see its management. Which characteristic is this?
slides.narration: Read the situation carefully and look for the clue about seeing and feeling.

slides.heading: Why management is important

visual.alt: Flow of five reasons why management is important: achieving group goals, increasing efficiency, creating a dynamic organisation, helping achieve personal objectives and developing society
visual.caption: Why management matters

slides.narration: Why does every organisation need management? It unites individual efforts towards group goals. It reduces waste and raises efficiency. It helps the organisation adapt to change. It helps employees meet their own goals through motivation and leadership. And by producing good goods, creating jobs and using new technology, it helps society develop.

slides.heading: Quick check: a group activity
slides.body_md: Decide whether the statement about management as a group activity is true or false.
slides.narration: Think about what an organisation is made of, and what management does with those people.

slides.heading: Is management a science?
columns:
**Yes, partly**

It has a systematic body of knowledge and principles drawn from observation and testing.

**But inexact**

Its principles deal with people, so the same principle can give different results.

rows: Not fully: results vary with human behaviour

visual.alt: Table testing management against three features of science: it has systematic knowledge and principles based on observation, but universal validity is not fully met, so it is an inexact science
visual.caption: Verdict: an inexact (soft) science.

slides.narration: A science has systematic knowledge, principles based on experiment, and results that hold everywhere. Management has the first two in some form. But because its principles deal with human behaviour, the same principle may work differently in two teams. So we call management an inexact, or soft, science.

slides.heading: Management as an art

rows: Each manager uses it in an own style
Skill grows with practice; new solutions

visual.alt: Table of three features of art and how management shows them: theoretical knowledge, personalised application and practice with creativity
visual.caption: Verdict: management is an art.

slides.narration: An art is the skilful, personal use of knowledge. Management fits well. There is plenty of theory to learn. Each manager applies it in an own style, so two managers handle the same problem differently. And skill improves with practice and creativity. So management is clearly an art.

slides.heading: Management as a profession

rows: Restricted entry (degree or licence by law)

visual.alt: Table testing five features of a profession: body of knowledge yes, restricted entry no, professional association partly, ethical code partly, service motive yes
visual.caption: Verdict: not yet a full profession.

slides.narration: A profession such as law or medicine has five features. Management has a body of knowledge and a service motive. But entry is not restricted by law: anyone can be appointed a manager. Associations exist, such as the All India Management Association, but joining is optional and its code has no legal force. So management is not yet a full profession.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: planning a 5-mark answer
slides.body_md: Question: Can management be called a profession?
bullets: Step 1: One line on what a profession is.
Step 2: Take the **five features** one by one.
Step 3: For each, write **met, not met or partly met**, with a reason.
Step 4: End with a clear **conclusion**.

visual.alt: Flow for structuring a five-mark answer: introduce, test each of the five features, say whether each is met, and conclude with a reason
visual.caption: Answer plan for a 5-mark question

slides.narration: Here is how to plan a five mark answer on the profession question. Start with one line on what a profession is. Then test the five features one at a time, saying whether each is met, not met or partly met, with a short reason. Finish with a clear conclusion. One feature, one mark, so keep each point separate and labelled.

slides.heading: Quick check: cost per fan
slides.body_md: An imagined fan maker made 1,200 fans on time for ₹54,000. Find the cost per fan.
slides.narration: Divide the total cost by the number of fans, then compare it with the planned cost per fan.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Getting work done effectively and efficiently
Goal-oriented, pervasive, multidimensional, continuous, group, dynamic, intangible
Art; inexact science; not a full profession

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: meaning of management, the three objectives, seven characteristics and the nature of management

slides.narration: Let us sum up. Management gets work done through others, effectively and efficiently. It serves organisational, social and personal objectives. It has seven characteristics, from goal oriented to intangible. It is important for the firm, its people and society. It is an art, an inexact science, and not yet a full profession.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: In cases, **quote the line** and then name and explain the concept.
Effectiveness is about **time and target**; efficiency is about **cost**.
For the profession question, test **all five** features and conclude.
Objectives: ask **whose** need is met.

rows: Effective: on time; efficient: low cost
It is the essence, present in all functions
Naming a concept without a quote in a case
Quote the exact line, then explain
Restricted entry and a binding code are missing

visual.alt: Exam tips table of four common mistakes and how to fix them

slides.narration: A few tips. In case questions, first quote the exact line, then name the concept and explain it. Keep effectiveness for time and target, and efficiency for cost. In the profession question, cover all five features and give a conclusion. To identify an objective, ask whose need is being met.

goals: Describe the three levels of management and the tasks of each
Explain and identify the five functions of management
Explain the meaning and characteristics of coordination
Analyse why coordination is needed and why it is the essence of management

slides.heading: Levels, functions and coordination
slides.body_md: Part 2: **who** manages, **what** managers do, and how **coordination** binds it all together.

slides.narration: In Part 1 we learnt what management is. Now we look inside an organisation. Who are the managers, and at what levels do they work? What functions do they perform? And what holds all their work together? The answer to the last question is coordination, often called the essence of management.

slides.narration: Managers work at three levels. At the top are the chairperson, chief executive and the board. In the middle are heads of departments such as production or finance. At the base are supervisors and foremen who work directly with the workers. Authority flows down this chain, while information and feedback flow both ways.

slides.heading: What each level does

rows: Goals and strategy; coordinate all departments; survival and social impact
Heads of production, finance, marketing, HR
Interpret policies; staff and assign duties; motivate; link with other departments
Oversee workers; quality and wastage; morale; pass problems upward

visual.alt: Table of the three levels of management with who belongs to each and their main tasks

slides.narration: Top management sets goals and strategy, coordinates all departments and is answerable for the survival of the firm and its impact on society. Middle management interprets these policies, staffs its departments, assigns duties and links with other departments. Supervisory management oversees the workers, keeps quality high and wastage low, maintains morale and carries workers problems upward.

visual.caption: The functions repeat as a cycle; coordination is the thread through all of them.

slides.narration: All managers perform five functions. Planning decides in advance what to do. Organising divides the work and gives authority and resources. Staffing finds and trains the right people. Directing leads, motivates and communicates. Controlling checks performance against the plan and corrects it. The cycle then starts again, with coordination running through all of it.

slides.heading: Functions at different levels
slides.body_md: Every manager performs **all five functions**; only the **time spent** on each differs.
bullets: Top managers spend more time on **planning and organising**.
Supervisors spend more time on **directing and controlling** daily work.

visual.alt: Table of how time spent on functions varies by level: top on planning and organising; middle on organising, staffing and directing; supervisory on directing and controlling

slides.narration: A common mistake is to think that only top managers plan and only supervisors direct. In fact every manager performs all five functions. What changes is the share of time. A chief executive spends more time on planning and organising. A supervisor spends more time guiding and checking the daily work of the team.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: naming the function
slides.body_md: Match each step of an imagined school annual day to a function.

headers: Step in an imagined school annual day
rows: Fix the date, events and budget
Form committees for stage, food and invitations
Pick and train compères and volunteers
Guide and encourage teams at rehearsals

visual.alt: Worked example table matching five steps of an imagined school annual day to the five functions: planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling
visual.caption: Look for the verb: decide, divide, hire, guide or check.

slides.narration: Let us use a school annual day. Fixing the date, events and budget is planning. Forming committees for the stage and food is organising. Picking and training compères is staffing. Guiding teams at rehearsals is directing. Comparing progress and spending with the plan is controlling. The verb in each step tells you the function.

slides.narration: Start with the function that comes before everything else, and end with the one that checks results.

slides.heading: What is coordination?
slides.body_md: **Coordination** is the process of **synchronising** the activities of different departments and people so that they work as one towards common goals.

nodes.label: Unity of action towards common goals

visual.alt: Flow showing departments of production, purchase, sales and finance brought together into unity of action towards common goals by coordination
visual.caption: Coordination synchronises departments

slides.narration: Imagine production makes more goods than sales can sell, or purchase buys material too late for production. Each department may be working hard, but not together. Coordination synchronises their timing, sequence and quantity, so that the whole organisation moves as one towards its goals. This unity of action is the purpose of coordination.

slides.heading: Characteristics of coordination

rows: Unites different interests into one purpose
All work towards a common goal
Consciously done; cooperation alone is not enough

visual.alt: Table of six characteristics of coordination and their meanings

slides.narration: Coordination integrates group efforts and ensures unity of action. It is continuous, beginning with planning and going on till controlling. It is all pervasive, needed in every department and at every level. It is the responsibility of every manager. And it is deliberate: even willing, friendly people need someone to consciously fit their work together.

slides.heading: Quick check: is it a separate function?
slides.body_md: Decide whether coordination is a separate sixth function of management.
slides.narration: Think about where coordination appears: in one function, or in all of them?

slides.heading: Why coordination is needed

nodes.label: Growth in size: more people, different goals
Specialisation: experts with their own views

visual.alt: Flow of three reasons that increase the need for coordination: growth in size, functional differentiation and specialisation
visual.caption: Why coordination is needed

slides.narration: Three things make coordination necessary. As an organisation grows in size, more people with different needs must be kept on the same path. Functional differentiation creates separate departments that may chase their own targets. And specialists tend to trust their own judgement. Each of these pulls the organisation apart unless coordination pulls it together.

slides.heading: The essence of management
columns:
**Not a separate function**

It is present in planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling.

**At every level**

Top, middle and supervisory managers all coordinate their teams.

sections.heading: 1. Meaning of management
sections.body_md:
Management is a **process** of getting things done **with and through people** so that goals are reached **effectively and efficiently**.

- **Effectiveness** — finishing the right task, on time (focus: result).
- **Efficiency** — using the least resources for that result (focus: cost and waste).

A unit can be effective without being efficient (target met, money wasted) or efficient without being effective (cheap, but late). Management seeks both.

key_terms.definition_md: Completing the task and achieving the target on time.
Achieving the result with minimum cost and resources.

sections.heading: 2. Objectives of management
sections.body_md:
- **Organisational:** survival (earn enough to cover costs), profit (reward for risk, funds for growth), growth (sales, employees, products, capital).
- **Social:** benefit for society — quality goods at fair prices, environment-friendly methods, employment for disadvantaged sections, community welfare.
- **Personal:** employees' financial needs (pay), social needs (recognition, good relations) and higher needs (growth).

In a case, identify the objective from **whose need** is met.

sections.heading: 3. Characteristics and importance
sections.body_md:
**Characteristics:** goal-oriented; pervasive (universal); multidimensional (work, people, operations); continuous; group activity; dynamic (adapts to change); intangible (felt through results).

**Importance:** it achieves group goals; increases efficiency; creates a dynamic organisation; helps people reach personal objectives; helps develop society (quality goods, jobs, new technology).

Changing in response to the environment.

sections.heading: 4. Science, art or profession?
sections.body_md:
- **Science:** has systematic knowledge and principles built from observation, but results vary with people — an **inexact (soft) science**.
- **Art:** theory exists, it is applied in a personal style, and skill grows with practice and creativity — management **is an art**.
- **Profession:** body of knowledge (yes), restricted entry by law (no), association (exists, e.g. AIMA, but optional), ethical code (no legal force), service motive (yes) — **not a full profession**.

sections.heading: 5. Levels and functions of management
sections.body_md:
**Levels:** top (chairperson, CEO, board: goals, strategy, survival, coordination of departments); middle (department heads: interpret policy, staffing, assigning duties, inter-department links); supervisory or operational (foremen, supervisors: oversee workers, quality, wastage, morale, pass problems up).

**Functions:** planning (decide in advance), organising (divide work, give authority and resources), staffing (right people in the right jobs, training), directing (lead, motivate, communicate, supervise), controlling (measure, compare with standards, correct). All levels perform all functions; time spent differs.

questions.stem_md: Which description best captures **management** as a process?

options.text_md: Doing all the work of an organisation personally to save costs
Getting work done through others so that goals are achieved effectively and efficiently
Keeping accounts of income and expenditure of a business
Selling goods at the highest possible price

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Getting work done through others so that goals are achieved effectively and efficiently. Management is a process of getting things done with and through people to reach goals effectively (on time) and efficiently (at least cost). Doing everything oneself, accounting and pricing are narrower activities, not the definition of management.

questions.stem_md: Sunrise Toys (an imagined firm in Jaipur) had to deliver 5,000 toys for a festival sale. It delivered all of them on time but spent much more on overtime and wasted material than budgeted. The firm was
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** effective but not efficient. Completing the task on time means it was effective; spending more than needed means it was not efficient (resources were wasted).

questions.stem_md: A courier unit of the imagined Kaveri Logistics cut its fuel and packing costs by a tenth, but missed the agreed delivery date for a hospital order. In terms of management, the unit was
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** efficient but not effective. Lower cost per unit shows efficiency; missing the deadline means the target was not achieved, so it was not effective.

questions.stem_md: An imagined cement company in Satna runs free eye-check camps for nearby villages and uses dust filters beyond legal requirements. Which objective of management does this reflect?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Social objective. Creating benefit for society, such as health camps and less pollution, is a social objective. Organisational objectives are survival, profit and growth; personal objectives relate to employees' needs.

questions.stem_md: Survival, profit and growth together form which category of management objectives?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Organisational objectives. The three organisational objectives are survival, profit and growth; they relate to the firm itself.

questions.stem_md: Management is needed in a hospital, a school, a temple trust and a cricket club alike. Which characteristic of management does this show?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Management is pervasive. Pervasive means universal: management is used in all kinds of organisations, economic or social, big or small, and in every country.

questions.stem_md: Visitors to the imagined Neelgiri Hotel cannot "see" its management, yet they notice that rooms are ready on time and staff work smoothly together. Which characteristic of management is highlighted?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It is an intangible force. Management cannot be seen; its presence is felt through results such as order, timeliness and satisfied guests. That is what intangible means.

questions.stem_md: Explain any five characteristics of management.
questions.solution_md: Any five characteristics, each with a short explanation.

answer.model_answer_md:

2. **Pervasive:** the same basic activities are needed in economic and social organisations alike, in small and large units, and in every country.
3. **Multidimensional:** it involves managing **work** (the tasks to be done), **people** (as individuals and as groups) and **operations** (turning inputs into outputs).
4. **Continuous:** the functions of planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling are performed again and again, and often together.

questions.solution_md: Test each feature of science and conclude.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Systematised body of knowledge:** management has its own principles and theories — **satisfied**.
2. **Principles based on experimentation:** they come from observation and repeated testing — **satisfied**, though tests involve people.
3. **Universal validity:** results vary because human behaviour is unpredictable — **not fully satisfied**. So management is an **inexact (soft) science**.

questions.stem_md: Evaluate whether management can be called a profession, examining each feature of a profession.
questions.solution_md: Five features each tested, with a reasoned conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:

3. **Professional association:** bodies such as **AIMA** exist, but membership is **not compulsory** — **not fully met**.
4. **Ethical code:** AIMA's code has **no legal force** — **not fully met**.

questions.stem_md: "Coordination is the essence of management." Analyse this statement and explain why the need for coordination arises in organisations.
questions.solution_md: Explain why coordination is the essence (two points) and three reasons for its need.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Essence:** coordination is not a separate function; it is the **force that binds** planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling, and is needed at **every level**.
2. **In each function:** e.g. in planning, departmental plans must fit the master plan; in controlling, actual results must match standards set together.
3. **Need — growth in size:** more people with different needs must be unified towards the organisation's goals.
4. **Need — functional differentiation:** departments such as finance and production may pursue their own objectives and must be linked.
5. **Need — specialisation:** specialists rely on their own judgement; coordination brings their work together.
So, without coordination, management would be a set of disconnected activities.

questions.stem_md: Which conclusion about the nature of management is the most accurate for India today?

options.text_md: It is an exact science like physics
It is an art and an inexact science, and it has some but not all features of a profession
It is a full profession like law, with compulsory licensing
It is neither an art nor a science, only common sense

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It is an art and an inexact science, and it has some but not all features of a profession. Management uses personal skill (art) and systematic but inexact principles (science); it lacks restricted entry and a binding code, so it is not yet a full profession.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Principles of management do not give exactly the same results in every situation.

**Reason (R):** They deal with human behaviour, which is not fully predictable.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: because people react differently, the outcome of applying a principle varies, which is why management is an inexact science.

answer.model_answer_md: A **top manager** spends more time on **planning** and organising, because he or she sets long-term goals for the whole firm. A **supervisor** spends more time on **directing**, because he or she works with the workers every day.

questions.stem_md: Explain these two features of coordination: it is a continuous process, and it is the responsibility of all managers.
questions.solution_md: One mark for each feature.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Continuous:** it begins at **planning** and goes on till **controlling**; it is never a one-time act.
2. **All managers:** each manager, from **top to supervisory level**, must synchronise the work of the people under him or her.
